result.summary: Pindar praises Chromios of Aitna for his chariot victory at Nemea, beginning with Ortygia and Sicily as a gift of Zeus to Persephone. He then turns to the myth of the infant Herakles strangling Hera's snakes and Teiresias' prophecy of his labors and eventual bliss on Olympus.

scenes.title: Editorial introduction to the ode
scenes.summary: The editor identifies Chromios, the date of the victory and the setting of the ode's performance.

scenes.title: Song at the house of Chromios
scenes.summary: Pindar hails Ortygia, praises Chromios' victory, recalls Sicily as Persephone's gift, and speaks of hospitality and generosity.

scenes.title: Infant Herakles and the snakes
scenes.summary: Hera sends two snakes to the newborn twins; Herakles strangles them, and Alkmene and Amphitryon rush in amazed.
scenes.stakes: The infant Herakles and his twin face death from Hera's snakes.

scenes.title: Teiresias prophesies Herakles' fate
scenes.summary: Teiresias foretells Herakles' victories over monsters and giants and his final rest and marriage to Hebe on Olympus.

alias_notes.explanation: Zeus worshipped in connection with the city of Aitna.

notable_quotes.reason: Pindar's counsel to follow one's own nature and walk straight paths.
Vivid image of the infant Herakles strangling the serpents.

analysis.text: The ode links Chromios' victory to Herakles, the model of inborn excellence. The myth shows nature and destiny shaping greatness.
Pindar celebrates Sicilian aristocratic patrons such as Hieron's circle, tying their prestige to heroic ancestry and Hieron's new city of Aitna.

legacy.text: The infant Herakles strangling snakes became a favorite subject in Greek and Roman art and later literature.

fun_facts.text: The ode was likely performed outside Chromios' house, as the text itself says Pindar 'stands at the doors of the hall'.

language_notes.text: Arethusa was a nymph who fled the river-god Alpheos and surfaced as a spring at Ortygia, linking Sicily to Greece's Alpheos river.
"Couch of Artemis" and "sister of Delos" call Ortygia a resting-place of the goddess and a twin of her birthplace, the island Delos.
Sicily was given to Persephone by Zeus as a wedding gift, according to tradition; bowing his hair means nodding assent.
Olympia's olive-leaves were the victor's crown at the Olympic games, so the Sicilians are praised as Olympic winners.
The "mouldering fire of reproach" means smouldering envy or blame, which Chromios' generous friends quench.
"Sons of Kadmos" are the Thebans, descended from Thebes' founder Kadmos.
Phlegra is where the gods fought the giants; Herakles aided them, since the giants could only be killed with a mortal's help.

context_notes.text: Hieron was the tyrant of Syracuse; Chromios was connected to him by marriage.
Hera, Zeus's wife, hated Herakles as the son of Zeus and the mortal Alkmene. His twin was Iphikles, son of Amphitryon.
Teiresias was the blind seer of Thebes, famous in Greek legend for his unfailing prophecies.

literary_notes.text: Poetic praise is imagined as shooting arrows at a target, a common Pindaric image of the poet's aim at truth.
The infant's instant strength and boldness establish Herakles as a hero from birth.
The general maxim about grief for one's own house turns Amphitryon's panic into a universal truth.
Teiresias' prophecy sketches Herakles' future labors, battle with the giants and final reward in Olympus.
